claims.text: The controlled material is a polycrystalline FCC high-entropy alloy initially having a random solid-solution state with minimal pre-existing SRO.
Sub-melting-temperature annealing can promote SRO formation in the HEA.
The proposed annealing treatment can increase SRO while leaving grain size and overall phase stability unchanged.
Rapid cooling minimizes SRO and preserves a near-ideal random solid solution.
The degree of short-range order is the structural mediator governing the proposed mechanical response.
Increased SRO raises the energy barrier and resistance experienced by moving dislocations, particularly leading partial dislocations.
Passage of a trailing partial after a leading partial can restore the FCC structure while creating a diffuse antiphase boundary through destruction of SRO on the slip plane.
The energy penalty associated with SRO disruption and antiphase-boundary generation produces back stress on moving dislocations.
SRO-associated back stress retards dislocation motion and enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Enhancing SRO increases the strength of the HEA.
Enhancing SRO increases the hardness of the HEA.
Relative to a random-solid-solution baseline, an SRO-enhanced HEA will have higher yield strength.
Relative to a random-solid-solution baseline, an SRO-enhanced HEA will have greater nanoindentation hardness.
The proposed mechanism applies to FCC-based HEAs in a dislocation-dominated plasticity regime.
Keeping grain size above the ultra-nanocrystalline range avoids grain-boundary-mediated softening and inverse Hall–Petch behavior that could obscure the SRO effect.
The hypothesis is limited to temperatures sufficiently below melting for SRO to form but not so low that other mechanisms become active.
Other microstructural factors, including grain size, may affect the measured strength and therefore obscure the magnitude attributable solely to SRO.
The strengthening response may vary with alloy composition and details of thermal treatment.
A lack of statistically significant increases in both yield strength and hardness in the SRO-promoted samples would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a correlation between SRO and impeded dislocation glide, antiphase boundaries, or back stress by TEM would falsify the proposed mechanism.
